The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus states that differentiation and integration are inverse operations. It has two parts. The first part says that if F is continuous and f is its derivative, then the definite integral from a to b of f of x equals F of b minus F of a. The second part says that differentiation undoes integration: the derivative with respect to x of the integral from a to x of f of t dt equals f of x. This theorem is the bridge connecting discrete sums to continuous accumulation, and it is arguably the most powerful result in calculus. By linking the rate of change of a function with its cumulative area, this theorem resolves the dual nature of calculus as originally conceived by Newton and Leibniz. It provides a practical, algebraic method for evaluating integrals without resorting to tedious limits of sums.

Part 1 tells us how to compute definite integrals. If f is continuous on the closed interval from a to b and F is any antiderivative of f—meaning F prime of x equals f of x—then the definite integral from a to b equals F of b minus F of a. This reduces the problem of computing a definite integral to finding an antiderivative, which is often much easier than computing the limit of Riemann sums directly.

Part 2 says that if f is continuous, then differentiating an integral recovers the integrand: the derivative with respect to x of the integral from a to x equals f of x. This tells us that integration and differentiation are inverse processes, at least for continuous functions. If the upper limit is not x but some function g of x, you must apply the chain rule, giving you the derivative with respect to x of the integral from a to g of x equals f of g of x times g prime of x.

The consequences are profound. The theorem transforms calculus from a computational tool into a unified framework. Answers to "how much accumulated?" can be found via antiderivatives. It enables applications across physics: total distance traveled equals the integral of velocity, total work done equals the integral of force, and total charge equals the integral of current. It explains why antiderivatives and indefinite integrals are related—they are, through this theorem.

The Fundamental Theorem is the pinnacle of elementary mathematics. Without it, integrals would be computed only through limit-of-sums approximations, which are slow and difficult. The connection between rate-of-change and total-accumulation would be mysterious. Historically, Newton and Leibniz independently discovered this theorem, and it was the key insight that unified their respective approaches to calculus. In quiz bowl, questions test whether you can state the theorem, apply it to evaluate definite integrals, or recognize scenarios where it applies.
